summary: For ages 7–9: contrast the Arctic and Antarctic by what lies UNDER the ice. The Arctic is an ocean basin whose central ice is floating sea ice, ringed by land (Canada, Russia, Greenland, Scandinavia); Antarctica is a continent larger than Europe, buried under ice more than 4 km thick in places and surrounded by the Southern Ocean. This structural difference helps explain a consequence chain — different conditions (Antarctica higher, colder, windier), different human presence (indigenous communities on the Arctic's connected land vs research stations only on isolated Antarctica), and no native land mammals in Antarctica. Wildlife also differs (polar bears, Arctic foxes, walruses in the Arctic; penguins, leopard seals, albatrosses in the Antarctic), partly because these animals live in one hemisphere and cannot cross the warm tropics, not because of land vs ocean alone. Learners sort animals, substrates and conditions to the correct pole WITH reasons, and explain how ocean-vs-land contributes to different life.
misconceptions: The Arctic and Antarctic are basically the same, just north and south — one is ocean, the other a high, thick-iced continent
Penguins and polar bears could meet — their species are confined to opposite poles
Both poles are equally cold — Antarctica is colder, higher and windier because it is a thick-ice continent
Antarctica's ice floats like the Arctic's — most Antarctic ice sits on land/bedrock, not on ocean
There's lots of land in the Arctic under the ice — the central Arctic ice floats on the Arctic Ocean

activities.title: Which pole? Sort with reasons and watch the consequences
steps: Study two side-by-side cross-sections: the Arctic showing the central sea ice FLOATING on dark ocean with land at the edges; Antarctica showing ice piled kilometres thick on solid rock, ringed by ocean.

Take a deck of cards — polar bear, penguin, walrus, albatross, Arctic fox, leopard seal, 'ocean underneath', 'rock/land underneath', 'colder & windier', 'people live here', 'research stations only' — and place each onto the correct world.

For each placement, state aloud or in writing the REASON ('penguins live only in the south', 'polar bears hunt seals from the Arctic's floating sea ice', 'the Arctic's land joins other continents, so people and land animals like Arctic foxes could reach it').
Name at least two countries bordering the Arctic, and compare Antarctica's size to Europe on a map.
activities.insight: The two poles are not just north/south twins: the Arctic is an ocean with land around it, Antarctica a thick-iced continent with ocean around it — that substrate difference helps explain how harsh each place is and why Antarctica has no native land mammals or indigenous people, while which animals live at each pole also depends on which hemisphere they come from.

activities.title: Cross-section reveal: what's under the ice?
steps: Look at two cross-sections side by side and tap each to reveal what lies beneath the ice at each pole.
Describe in your own words what you would hit if you drilled straight down at the North Pole (floating sea ice, then ocean) versus the South Pole (kilometres of ice, then solid rock/land).
State which pole is the ocean and which is the continent, naming the Southern Ocean and at least two Arctic-bordering lands.
activities.insight: The surface of both poles looks the same (ice and cold), but the substrate does not: central Arctic = ice on ocean; Antarctic = ice on thick land.

activities.title: Two polar guides describe their home
steps: Take the role of an Arctic guide and an Antarctic guide (or have two speakers) who each describe their pole's substrate, wildlife, conditions and human presence.
Each guide must state one reason their pole supports the life it does (e.g. 'surrounding land and frozen sea let polar bears and people live here').
Afterwards, write or say two differences in human presence: indigenous peoples in the Arctic vs research stations only in Antarctica.
activities.insight: Articulating each pole's features aloud, including the reasons, is intended to reinforce that geography (land vs ocean) helps explain the differing conditions and inhabitants.

activities.title: Compare-the-poles check questions
steps: Answer 'which pole?' categorisation items for animals and features.

Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'Both the Arctic and Antarctic are ice-covered and freezing. A student says they're basically the same underneath — both frozen sea at the top and bottom of the world. Is what's UNDER the ice the same? Explain the big difference, and how it helps explain why people have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years but only visit research stations in Antarctica.'
activities.insight: A learner with the concept identifies ocean-under-ice (Arctic) vs land-under-ice (Antarctic) AND uses it to explain differences in conditions and human presence; a learner seeing only 'ice and cold' calls the poles the same.

checkQuestion: Both the Arctic and the Antarctic are ice-covered and freezing. A student says 'so underneath the ice they're basically the same — both are frozen sea at the top of and bottom of the world.' Is what's UNDER the ice the same at both poles? Explain the big difference, and why it means people and polar bears can live at one pole but not the other.
checkAnswer: No — what's underneath is completely different. The ARCTIC is an OCEAN covered by floating sea ice, with land around its edges (Canada, Russia, Greenland, Scandinavia). ANTARCTICA is a CONTINENT — solid land bigger than Europe — buried under ice up to about 4 km thick, surrounded by ocean. That difference explains the life: the Arctic's surrounding land and frozen sea support polar bears, Arctic foxes, walruses and human communities (like the Inuit), while Antarctica's isolated, ice-buried land has penguins, leopard seals and albatrosses but no permanent human residents and no land mammals.
